highlightAliases.old: Lactulose/sorbitol — 15-30 mL/day; adds 1.9 BM/wk (p1376); sorbitol equally effective and cheaper.
highlightAliases.new: Lactulose/sorbitol — 15–30 mL once or twice daily (Table 87-9, p1373); adds 1.9 BM/wk (p1376); sorbitol equally effective and cheaper.

highlightAliases.old: Rome IV: ≥2 of the following, on >25% of occasions, for ≥12 wk in the last 12 mo: ≤2 BM/week, straining, hard stool (Bristol 1-2), sensation of incomplete evacuation, sensation of anorectal obstruction, manual maneuvers to defecate (p1354).
highlightAliases.new: Rome IV functional constipation requires at least two features: straining, hard or lumpy stool (Bristol 1–2), incomplete evacuation, anorectal blockage, manual maneuvers (each in more than 25% of defecations), or fewer than 3 spontaneous bowel movements/week; criteria must be met during the last 3 months, with onset at least 6 months before diagnosis, rare loose stools without laxatives and insufficient criteria for IBS (Rome Foundation, C2); Hazzard Table 87-1 prints 12 weeks in the last 12 months (p1354).

highlightAliases.old: Normal perineal descent is <4 cm (p1365). Plain x-ray: megacolon = colon diameter >6.5 cm; rectal dilatation >4 cm implies dysmotility (p1365).
highlightAliases.new: Normal perineal descent is <4 cm (p1365). Plain x-ray: colon diameter >6.5 cm without acute obstruction points toward megacolon; rectal dilatation >4 cm implies dysmotility (p1365).

highlightAliases.old: Senna — 1-3 tabs at bedtime; onset 8-12 h (p1372); cheap, safe first-line stimulant.
highlightAliases.new: Senna — 1-3 tabs at bedtime if symptoms persist after bulk laxatives in ambulant older people (Table 87-11, p1378); onset 8-12 h (p1372); cheap, safe first-line stimulant.

highlightAliases.old: PEG — more potent hyperosmolar laxative than lactulose; disimpaction regimen 1 L (8 sachets)/day × 3 days achieved 89% success (p1376); caution: liquid stools.
highlightAliases.new: PEG — more potent hyperosmolar laxative than lactulose; a trial of PEG plus electrolytes for disimpaction at 1 L (8 sachets)/day × 3 days achieved 89% success (p1376); caution: liquid stools.

highlightAliases.old: ≥2 of: ≤2 BM/wk, straining, hard stool (Bristol 1-2), incomplete evacuation, anorectal obstruction sensation, manual maneuvers — on >25% of occasions for ≥12 wk in the last 12 mo (p1354).
highlightAliases.new: At least two features: fewer than three spontaneous bowel movements/week, or straining, Bristol 1–2 stools, incomplete evacuation, blockage or manual maneuvers in more than 25% of defecations; symptoms fulfill criteria for the last three months and began at least six months before diagnosis, loose stools are rare without laxatives, and IBS criteria are insufficient (Rome Foundation, C2); Table 87-1 (p1354) gives a different time window.

highlightAliases.old: Rome IV: ≥2 of the following, on >25% of occasions, for ≥12 wk in the last 12 mo: ≤2 BM/week, straining, hard stool (Bristol 1-2), sensation of incomplete evacuation, sensation of anorectal obstruction, manual maneuvers to defecate; loose stools rarely occur without laxatives and IBS criteria are not fulfilled (p1354).
highlightAliases.new: Rome IV functional constipation requires at least two features: straining, hard or lumpy stool (Bristol 1–2), incomplete evacuation, anorectal blockage, manual maneuvers (each in more than 25% of defecations), or fewer than 3 spontaneous bowel movements/week; criteria must be met during the last 3 months, with onset at least 6 months before diagnosis, rare loose stools without laxatives and insufficient criteria for IBS (Rome Foundation, C2); Hazzard Table 87-1 prints 12 weeks in the last 12 months (p1354).

highlightAliases.old: <3 BM/week carries a >2-fold colon cancer risk in adjusted studies — constipation itself is not an indication for colonoscopy, but a genuine change in bowel habit should prompt workup (p1361).
highlightAliases.new: In one adjusted study, reporting <3 BM/week was associated with >2-fold colon cancer risk — constipation itself is not an indication for colonoscopy, but a genuine change in bowel habit should prompt workup (p1361).

highlightAliases.old: Biofeedback outperforms laxatives/diazepam for rectal outlet delay/dyssynergia: 70% vs 23% response at 3 months, 80% vs 22% at 6-12 months (p1371).
highlightAliases.new: For dyssynergic defecation, biofeedback improved symptoms in 70% vs 23% with diazepam at 3 months; in a separate comparison, 80% vs 22% improved with biofeedback versus laxatives at both 6 and 12 months (p1371).

highlightAliases.old: ≥2 of: ≤2 BM/wk, straining, hard stool (Bristol 1-2), incomplete evacuation, anorectal obstruction sensation, manual maneuvers — on >25% of occasions for ≥12 wk in the last 12 mo; loose stools rarely occur without laxatives and IBS criteria are not fulfilled (p1354).
highlightAliases.new: At least two features: fewer than three spontaneous bowel movements/week, or straining, Bristol 1–2 stools, incomplete evacuation, blockage or manual maneuvers in more than 25% of defecations; symptoms fulfill criteria for the last three months and began at least six months before diagnosis, loose stools are rare without laxatives, and IBS criteria are insufficient (Rome Foundation, C2); Table 87-1 (p1354) gives a different time window.

highlightAliases.old: Table 87-9 laxative mechanisms (owner-highlighted): sodium picosulfate is hydrolyzed by colonic bacteria, bisacodyl by intestinal/colonic brush-border enzymes — both to the same active metabolite (antiabsorptive/secretory, prokinetic); sorbitol/lactulose are nonabsorbable disaccharides metabolized by colonic bacteria to short-chain fatty acids; PEG osmotically increases intraluminal fluids; senna/anthraquinones alter electrolyte transport via increased intraluminal fluids, stimulate the myenteric plexus, and increase motility (p1373–1374).
highlightAliases.new: Table 87-9 laxative mechanisms (owner-highlighted): sodium picosulfate is hydrolyzed by colonic bacteria, bisacodyl by intestinal/colonic brush-border enzymes — both to the same active metabolite (antiabsorptive/secretory, prokinetic); lactulose is a nonabsorbed disaccharide fermented by colonic bacteria, while sorbitol is an osmotic sugar alcohol; PEG osmotically increases intraluminal fluids; senna/anthraquinones alter electrolyte transport via increased intraluminal fluids, stimulate the myenteric plexus, and increase motility (p1373–1374).

highlightAliases.old: Diabetes: colonic transit prolongs to 200 ± 144 h in immobile diabetics. If using metoclopramide, older adults should avoid continuous treatment for longer than 12 weeks, with a 2-week drug holiday or a dose decrease as tolerated (tardive dyskinesia risk) (p1361).
highlightAliases.new: Diabetes: colonic transit prolongs to 200 ± 144 h in immobile diabetics. Metoclopramide may treat diabetic gastroparesis. Tardive dyskinesia risk rises with total exposure. For diabetic gastroparesis, US prescribing information advises avoiding more than 12 weeks of total treatment. A drug holiday does not reset cumulative exposure (p1361). Reglan prescribing information, Boxed Warning

highlightAliases.old: PAMORAs for opioid-induced constipation — naldemedine (52% vs 35% achieving >3 CSBM vs placebo) and naloxegol (42% vs 29% achieving ≥3 CSBM/wk) (p1378).
highlightAliases.new: PAMORAs for opioid-induced constipation — naldemedine and naloxegol counter opioid effects in the gut. Pooled response rates on p1378 are 52% vs 35% and 42% vs 29%, respectively. The pivotal trials measured spontaneous bowel movements, without requiring a sense of complete evacuation. Responders had at least three per week and at least one more than baseline for nine of twelve weeks, including three of the last four. COMPOSE trials · KODIAC trials

highlightAliases.old: Why must metoclopramide use in older adults be time-limited, and beyond what duration should continuous treatment be avoided?
highlightAliases.new: Why must metoclopramide use in older adults be time-limited, and what total duration should generally be avoided for diabetic gastroparesis?

highlightAliases.old: Risk of tardive dyskinesia is increased in older adults; avoid continuous treatment for longer than 12 weeks.
highlightAliases.new: Older adults are particularly susceptible to tardive dyskinesia, which may be irreversible. For diabetic gastroparesis, avoid more than 12 weeks of total treatment.

highlightAliases.old: A 2-week drug holiday or a decrease of metoclopramide dose as tolerated (with tight blood glucose control) is encouraged whenever clinically possible (p1361).
highlightAliases.new: Interrupting treatment or reducing the dose does not erase previous exposure (p1361 and the Reglan boxed warning above).
